A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Ar2Can research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be reliably matched despite additions and pagination changes.

before.justification: V2 reports original benchmark experiments, component ablations, training curves, latency measurements, and qualitative generation results.

after.justification: V3 retains those original results and adds a human preference study, additional Architect comparisons, and object-generation examples.

M1.justification: V3 introduces the BAGEL-based Architect-C alternative, fine-tuned using Architect-B's GRPO procedure (Section 3.3.2 and Appendix D.6). The existing Architect-A/B, Artist, rewards, matching, token handling, and curriculum remain unchanged. Newly disclosed LoRA and preprocessing details do not establish changes to the earlier procedure.

E1.justification: Training data sources and the MultiHuman-Testbench and Multi-ID-Test benchmarks are retained. Appendix E.8 adds limited qualitative coverage of multi-object and mixed human/object generation, including appearance editing and occlusion, without additional object-data training.

E2.justification: Table D.6 adds RPG/LayoutGPT-style layout generators using GPT-4o and Llama as Architect replacements feeding the same Artist. Existing benchmark comparator sets are retained; Dream-O/DreamO and X-Verse/XVerse are naming changes. The new preference study compares against the already evaluated DreamO and XVerse.

E3.justification: V3 extends evaluation beyond automated benchmarks with 25 evaluators assessing 25 triplets containing 3–5 identities on prompt alignment, identity preservation, and quality (Table 4). It also introduces RMS Spread for layout evaluation and controlled Architect replacements using the same Artist (Tables D.5–D.6). Previously reported benchmark settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test specialist Architects against unified BAGEL and off-the-shelf layout generators, examine HPSv3 removal from Architect-B, and explore generalization to objects (Appendices D.6–D.7 and E.7–E.8). These substantially broaden the questions investigated beyond v2's retained sorting, matching, curriculum, reward-weight, and token-sharing analyses.

E5.justification: V3 adds no repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures. Existing plots retain their uncertainty presentation. The new evaluator count describes the user-study sample rather than repeated model runs or uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Existing scores in Tables 1–3 and D.2–D.4 are unchanged. New results include 88% prompt wins for Ar2Can versus 4% for DreamO and 8% for XVerse (Table 4), Architect-C's final ID score of 68.0 and 27-second layout generation (Table D.5), and off-the-shelf Architect results (Table D.6). V3 also adds RMS Spread measurements, the 0.07-to-0.02 drop without Architect-B's HPSv3 reward, and object-generation outputs. These are additional findings, not performance improvements over v2 under unchanged settings.

T1.justification: Appendix D.2 newly defines RMS Spread as the root mean square of pairwise distances between predicted bounding-box centers. This is a limited mathematical-definition addition. Existing equations, matching rules, pose formulations, and training algorithms are unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the principal claims: separating spatial planning from identity rendering, two preferred Architect variants, compositional GRPO rewards, efficient token handling, and strong multi-human generation using synthetic multi-person training data. Added supporting experiments do not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations connecting curriculum training to stability, HPSv3 to prevention of layout reward hacking, and layout diversity and computational cost to Architect selection. Appendix E.8 interprets object examples as evidence of broader compositional generalization. The limitations concerning expression control, complex actions, and larger groups remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix B.3 newly specifies rank-64 LoRA training for Architect-B and the Artist. New Appendix C.3 describes inference-time face segmentation, landmark alignment, and canvas placement; the abstract adds a project-page pointer. These improve documentation without establishing that previously reported training or preprocessing was changed, or that code was released.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning against directly relevant alternatives. It adds LayoutGPT/RPG and concurrent Canvas-to-Image/LayerComposer, distinguishing Ar2Can through specialized Architect training and synthetic multi-human data, and explicitly credits Flow-GRPO. Additional personalization and unified-model references broaden the context beyond bibliographic corrections.

P1.justification: V3 edits the abstract and introductory prose, consolidates and rewrites related work, expands several explanations, and adds appendix subsections and an LLM-use disclosure. The main narrative order and most method and appendix text remain intact.

P2.justification: V3 adds Table 4, Tables D.5–D.6, Figures E.8–E.9, and an RMS Spread column in Table D.1. Existing figure images are retained, several captions are shortened, and tables and text are reflowed, including moving Table 2 from page 8 to page 7. The established visual design remains.

improvement.justification: The new Architect comparisons strengthen the justification for the design, while the LoRA and inference-canvas disclosures improve reproducibility. The preference study adds human evidence, although its criterion-score scale and aggregation are underspecified, and object generalization remains qualitative. These provide a limited net improvement around otherwise unchanged core benchmark evidence.
